title: Acute effects of almond milk vs. almond milk supplemented with almond protein powder or whey protein on plasma amino acid profiles and hydration status in postmenopausal women: a randomised crossover study protocol

sections.abstract:
Postmenopausal women experience hormonal changes that negatively impact muscle mass, hydration, and metabolic health. Optimising protein intake during this life stage can mitigate musculoskeletal function declines, yet many consume inadequate protein. As interest grows in choosing sustainable, plant-based alternatives over animal protein, almond protein powder (APP), a by-product of almond oil extraction, presents a novel option for consumers. Differing from a protein isolate, APP retains fat, fibre, and micronutrients, which may influence its potential for promoting muscle protein synthesis and hydration. However, little is known about APP’s acute physiological effects, or perceived responses such as fullness/satiety, taste or gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. This study aims to investigate the postprandial amino acid, glycaemic, insulinemic, hydration, and perceived responses to APP in postmenopausal women, comparing it to a whey protein supplement. Findings will inform tailored supplementation strategies for an underrepresented and nutritionally vulnerable population in the future.

This protocol paper details a randomised, crossover study of 14 postmenopausal women, assessing the acute amino acid profile and hydration responses in postmenopausal women following ingestion of APP as compared to whey protein, water or almond milk. Venous blood, urine and questionnaires are to be collected during each session for 180 min post-ingestion. Primary outcomes include aminoacidemia (total amino acids, as well as all 20 individual primary amino acids) and hydration markers (urine volume excreted, body mass, plasma volume, urine specific gravity, urine colour, plasma osmolality, fluid retention). Secondary outcomes include perceived appetite, thirst, gastrointestinal symptoms, and supplement tolerability and acceptability. Between-treatment comparisons will be made using linear mixed models with a fixed effect of treatment and a random intercept for participant.

The study strengths include a focus on postmenopausal women, an underrepresented group in clinical and nutrition research who are susceptible to problems with muscle function and hydration. The use of a randomised crossover design to reduce inter-individual variability strengthens this study further. A combination of objective measures and subjective responses offers insights into both physiological effects and consumer acceptability of APP versus whey protein. Hydration assessment is particularly relevant given the postmenopausal population can be at increased risk of fluid imbalance. Acute measurement of responses to APP limit the transferability to longer-term supplementation, and there are some inherent macronutrient discrepancies between treatments which may influence glycaemic and insulinemic responses to supplementation.

DUHREC: 2024/ HE000669 , ANZCTR: ACTRN12625000127404p.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12937-025-01226-1.
sections.introduction:
The menopause transition is characterised by substantial reductions in reproductive hormones, particularly the cessation of hormone cycling leading to the permanent loss of menstrual periods. In medical terms, twelve months after the final menstrual period, women are classed as being post-menopausal [ 1 ]. The loss of ovarian function and resulting change in the hormonal milieu is believed to be a contributing factor to the adverse alterations in body composition and metabolism that drive reductions in cardiovascular and musculoskeletal health post menopause [ 2 , 3 ]. Weight gain and loss of muscle mass and function [ 4 ] are particularly relevant during this phase, increasing the risk and impact of obesity-related health issues [ 5 ] and risk of falls.

Postmenopausal women have lower estrogen levels when compared to premenopausal women [ 6 ], which impacts fat and protein metabolism [ 7 ], as well as fluid balance [ 8 ]. The postmenopausal hormonal changes may be part of what blunts the response of postmenopausal muscle to anabolic stimuli [ 5 ] when compared to muscle in younger females or older males [ 9 – 11 ]. This means that postmenopausal women may require a higher protein intake to achieve comparable anabolic effects to premenopausal counterparts. However, women in the postmenopausal age group have been reported to consume less protein than younger women [ 4 ]. Higher protein intakes in this population are associated with improved muscle function and physical performance [ 4 , 12 ]. These changes highlight the importance of optimised protein intake strategies in this population.

Consumer reports demonstrate that protein is high on the agenda for many countries and there is increasing interest in plant-based diets and plant-based sources of protein [ 13 ]. Replacing animal protein with plant protein has become an important objective to reduce greenhouse gas emissions for high-income nations [ 14 ]. These trends to transition away from animal protein and towards plant protein is supported by the EAT-LANCET's commission on healthy diets from sustainable food systems [ 15 ]. The EAT-LANCET recommendations emphasise whole plant foods like vegetables, nuts, and grains rather than isolated protein sources. In contexts where achieving adequate protein intake from whole foods alone may be challenging, such as in older adults or clinical populations, plant-based protein powders offer a convenient and concentrated source of dietary protein. When evaluated for anabolic potential, plant-based proteins generally stimulate lower muscle protein synthesis (MPS) responses as compared to animal-based protein isolates [ 16 – 18 ]. However, protein isolates are not reflective of how that protein performs as part of a whole food matrix. For example, whole eggs are more anabolic than egg whites [ 19 ] and whole milk is more anabolic that skimmed milk [ 20 ]. These data suggest that fat in the matrix of the food may have a potentiating effect on the protein’s anabolic response.

A case in point is evidence indicating that almond protein powder (APP), despite being plant based, is comparable to whey protein isolate at maintaining nitrogen balance in young women [ 21 ]. Although nitrogen balance is not necessarily a direct reflection of skeletal muscle protein balance, it is suggestive that APP may have anabolic properties like whey protein. APP may more closely mimic whole foods than other protein isolates, because it contains additional nutrients such as ~ 13% fat, ~ 18% fibre and other micronutrients. The slowing of gastric emptying associated with protein and fibre intake may help attenuate postprandial glucose excursions [ 22 ], which is particularly beneficial for metabolically at-risk populations such as postmenopausal women. So, whilst APP is not a complete source of amino acids [ 23 ], it may still have significant anabolic and metabolic potential.

APP is a by-product of the almond oil extraction industry where the fat component of the almonds is cold pressed out leaving a defatted almond cake which can be finely milled to a powder suitable for adding to food such as protein shakes. In addition to supporting improvements in lean mass and strength when combined with resistance training [ 24 ], dietary protein also plays a role in weight management and body composition modification, due to its satiating effect [ 25 ]. APP offers a unique nutritional composition, including a high fibre content as compared to protein isolates, as well as a significant fraction of monounsaturated fats, which are associated with improved heart health and lipid profiles [ 26 ]. Indeed, plant-protein consumption is associated with improved heart health, likely due to the content of plant derived bioactives found in plant proteins [ 27 ]. However, little is known about the acute physiological responses to ingestion of APP, potentially limiting the precision of recommendations for its implementation.

Assessing circulating insulin and glucose following ingestion of APP is also relevant given the increased prevalence of insulin resistance and impaired glucose metabolism among postmenopausal women [ 28 ]. Estrogen deficiency contributes to decreased insulin sensitivity and altered glucose homeostasis, increasing cardiometabolic risk during the postmenopausal years [ 29 ]. Protein ingestion, especially when combined with dietary fibre and fat, such as that found in APP, can influence postprandial insulin and glucose dynamics [ 30 ]. Understanding how APP impacts these parameters is valuable to evaluate suitability for this population, in terms of anabolic potential and in managing metabolic risk factors.

A protein supplement delivered in the form of a liquid shake not only presents an opportunity to boost muscle maintenance/growth but also could contribute to improved hydration status. Dehydration can present health risks for postmenopausal women, including impaired cognitive and physical function in some cases [ 31 ]. Considering the role that estrogen plays in regulating thirst [ 32 ], postmenopausal women are more likely to under-consume fluid for adequate hydration. This demographic also reports a greater level of urinary concern or incontinence than premenopausal women [ 33 ], and may intentionally limit fluid intake as a result. The negative effect of age on renal function is established [ 34 ], so we may also expect that postmenopausal women experience impaired fluid retention. Accordingly, consideration should be paid to the hydration impact of dietary supplementation strategies when providing recommendations to postmenopausal women (i.e. selection of APP or an alternative protein powder such as whey). With these health considerations in mind, identifying if APP can provide adequate nutrition properties to suggest maintenance of MPS (assessed by acute aminoacidemia monitoring), while also facilitating adequate hydration, warrants investigation.

Several factors such as the age of the participant, the dose, digestibility and amino acid composition of the protein source influence the effectiveness of a protein source in terms of its ability to induce anabolic processes in skeletal muscle [ 35 ]. As MPS is closely linked to the postprandial rise in circulating amino acids (aminoacidemia) [ 35 , 36 ], characterising this acute metabolic response to the ingested protein such as the insulinogenic, glycaemic, and fluid retention responses is important to evaluating the potential efficacy of a particular protein supplement. Additional assessments of participant perceptions such as tolerability, gastrointestinal symptoms and satiation have implications for dietary protein supplementation in postmenopausal women, in that a supplementation protocol that is well tolerated may be more likely to be adhered to.

Understanding the effects of APP ingestion on aminoacidemia, insulin, glucose, hydration status, and perceived responses in postmenopausal women may provide insight into the potential efficacy of APP as a protein supplement. Clarifying the acute response to APP ingestion is foundational for understanding the impacts that are observed in other longer-term supplementation studies or in expensive and invasive tracer-based studies of muscle metabolism. From a consumer selection perspective, APP may offer an alternative for individuals with dietary restrictions, such as those avoiding animal-based proteins due to allergies, ethical beliefs, or lifestyle choices. By evaluating the efficacy of APP as a viable protein source in comparison to other readily available protein supplements (whey), we may offer consumers with more options that provide comparable or potentially even better effects. Ultimately, this research will address gaps in our understanding of how almond derived nutrients (proteins, healthy fats, and fibre) are handled in the few hours after supplementation in an under-represented population.

This may facilitate understanding of how and why APP ingestion elicits acute responses that characterise proposed longer-term responses to supplementation in postmenopausal women, which are to be assessed in other investigations. It seeks to address these points, via the following primary and secondary objectives.

Primary objectives: Assess aminoacidemia and hydration status changes in postmenopausal women, in response to ingestion of APP as compared to whey protein, almond milk or water.

Secondary objectives: Assess insulin and glycaemic responses, as well as subjective ratings of APP in postmenopausal women, as compared to whey protein, almond milk or water. Subjective ratings include assessments of hunger, thirst, gastrointestinal symptoms and taste tolerability.
sections.methods:
This randomised crossover study will be conducted within the Institute for Physical Activity and Nutrition (IPAN) at Deakin University (Melbourne, Australia). This design allows investigation of the primary research questions identified for this study; the acute amino acid profile and hydration responses in postmenopausal women following ingestion of APP as compared to whey protein dissolved in almond milk, or water or almond milk alone. The SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2013 statement was used in designing this study protocol [ 37 ]. The SPIRIT Checklist is included as Additional File 1, and the SPIRIT Diagram is included as Fig. 1 . Participants will be eligible for inclusion in the study if they meet all the following criteria: Biological female at birth. Aged 50 to 65 years. Have undergone natural menopause (no menstrual bleeding for 12 consecutive months). Body mass index (BMI) between 18 and 35 kg.m 2 . Body mass stable over the two months prior to participation (change not exceeding 2 kg). Stable use, or non-use, of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for the six months prior to participation.

Individuals will be excluded from participation in this study if they meet any of the following criteria: Known nut allergy. History of myopathic, neuropathic, skeletal, thrombotic, or cardiovascular disorders. Anticipated absence from the study for more than one week. Current smoker. Current chronic disease, including but not limited to cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic liver or kidney disease, or gastrointestinal disorders affecting nutrient absorption. Adherence to a vegan diet. Currently supplementing with a protein powder.

Two sample size calculations, performed using the ‘power package’ in Stata SE18 (StataCorp, Texas, United States of America), were conducted using inputs derived from previously published studies assessing the link between hydration and cognition in older adults [ 38 ], and aminoacidemia following protein ingestion in older women [ 39 ]. Informed by both power calculations, nine participants are required, and 14 participants will be recruited. This strategy more than accounts for dropout rates reported in supplement studies in older adults which can average up to 14% [ 40 ], thus providing an analysis sample of at least nine participants in the current study. Post-hoc power calculations will be conducted to verify that power was achieved and maintained.

Across both calculations, the following standard parameters were used: Power equal to or exceeding 0.80 Alpha (α) = 0.017 (nominal p < 0.05 with Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons) Within participant correlation values for outcomes were not reported in the cited studies, so a conservative correlation value of 0.75 was employed across both calculations.

Power equal to or exceeding 0.80

Alpha (α) = 0.017 (nominal p < 0.05 with Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons)

Within participant correlation values for outcomes were not reported in the cited studies, so a conservative correlation value of 0.75 was employed across both calculations.

Bethancourt and colleagues [ 38 ] reported data linking hydration status to cognitive performance in older adults. While their values are reported in osmolarity units (mmol·L⁻ 1 ), we can also interpret these as plasma osmolality (mmol·kg⁻ 1 ) in clinical human research, as the difference between the two is negligible in dilute solutions like plasma due to its density (~ 1.0 kg·L⁻ 1 ). Based on Bethancourt and colleagues’ findings that participants with plasma osmolality between 285 and 289 mmol·kg⁻ 1 significantly outperformed those with values < 285 or > 300, a meaningful difference may be interpreted as 5 mmol·kg⁻ 1 . Assuming a standard deviation of 5.2 mmol·kg⁻ 1 [ 38 ], a sample of n = 9 would provide sufficient power to detect a minimum mean difference of 5 mmol·kg⁻ 1 between conditions.

Oikawa and colleagues [ 39 ] reported that whey protein led to higher plasma leucine and myofibrillar MPS in older women compared to collagen protein. Post-ingestion, the difference between the whey and collagen groups for plasma leucine concentrations was 160 uM, with a standard deviation of 150 uM. Based on these outcomes [ 39 ] and the parameters above, a sample size of n = 8 would provide sufficient power to detect a minimum mean difference of 160 uM between conditions.

Participants will be recruited via a multi-modal strategy, leveraging social media and local community networks. Recruitment advertisements will be distributed through platforms such as Facebook and Instagram by members of the research team, accompanied by digital recruitment posters. Additionally, printed materials will be posted in community hubs. Individuals expressing interest will be contacted via email and provided with a plain language statement (PLS) outlining study aims, procedures, risks, and benefits. Recruitment is expected to occur until the required sample size is achieved.

An experimental testing session overview is provided in Fig. 2 . In short, 14 postmenopausal women, aged 50–65 years, will complete four testing sessions each, over approximately three to four weeks. Each of these experimental testing sessions will comprise the same protocol, with the only variation between sessions being the ingested treatment/supplement. Fig. 2 Schematic of experimental testing session overview, illustrating the data collection processes completed during each of the four treatments

Schematic of experimental testing session overview, illustrating the data collection processes completed during each of the four treatments

During each testing session, blood samples will be collected via intravenous cannulation from the antecubital vein by a certified research staff member, with samples taken twice at baseline (mean values to be reported), and at multiple intervals up to three hours post-ingestion (15 to 180 min) to assess hydration status and amino acid profiles.

At all collection time points, blood will be drawn into an EDTA coated vacutainer tube with collected volume approximating 8 mL. This sample is to be immediately centrifuged at 4500 RPM for 10 min, at 4° C. Plasma collected into Eppendorf tubes will be stored in −80° C freezers for later analyses of aminoacidemia. At baseline, 60-, 120-, and 180-min post-ingestion, blood will also be drawn into a lithium-heparin coated vacutainer tube, with collected volume approximating 2 mL. Aliquots from this whole blood sample will be immediately analysed for haematocrit and haemoglobin (facilitating plasma volume calculation), and for glucose. Remaining whole blood will be centrifuged at 3600 RPM for 10 min at 4° C, with plasma collected into cuvettes and immediately analysed for plasma osmolality.

Participants will be asked to void their bladder of all urine at baseline and at 60, 120, and 180 min to assess hydration through volume and specific markers. If participants do not void any urine, no measures are performed. If participants need to void prior to these times, they are free to do so, with the assessments performed at the times mentioned (i.e. all urine collected between 60–120 min is assessed at the 120 min mark).

Body mass will be measured at the same intervals to monitor fluid retention (body mass scales, IC-UC-321; A&D Co., Ltd; Tokyo, Japan), and bioelectrical impedance analysis will be used at baseline to assess resting total body water. Participants will complete questionnaires throughout each session to assess perceived responses to supplement ingestion.

For each session, participants will arrive in the morning after an overnight fast (no food or drink except water after 10 pm the night before, minimum of eight hours fasted). Participants will replicate their diet and exercise for the 24 h prior to each session (as verified via the use of the EasyDietDiary application, Version 6.0.28; Xyris Software; Brisbane, Australia) and will avoid alcohol and the use of saunas. We will ask participants to drink 500 mL water within a 30 min period, to be completed one hour before arrival at the laboratory, seeking euhydration at the commencement of all sessions. Fasting and water ingestion will be verified verbally upon participant arrival. Throughout these sessions, we will ask participants to remain seated within the laboratory (except when attending the bathroom or collecting body composition measures), during which time they are able to complete sedentary tasks such as reading or watching television. A washout period of at least two full days will be enforced between testing sessions, to allow recovery from any bruising which may occur with blood collection. Responses recorded in the current study are likely to be transient and acute [ 41 , 42 ], rendering this minimum washout period sufficient.

Aminoacidemia changes from baseline, as assessed via measurement of plasma concentrations of total amino acids (TAA), branched-chain amino acids (BCAA), essential amino acids (EAA), and all 20 primary amino acids. Amino acid concentrations will be measured via gold standard isotope dilution mass spectrometry, specifically gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, as previously described [ 43 ]. Amino acid concentrations will be assessed at baseline twice (to verify reproducibility of resting values), and then 15-, 30-, 45-, 60-, 90-, 120- and 180-min post-ingestion.

Hydration status changes from baseline, as assessed via the following measurements. Urine mass excreted (g, MII-2500; Universal Weight Electronics; Geldermalsen, The Netherlands), body mass (kg, IC-UC-321; A&D Co., Ltd; Tokyo, Japan), plasma volume change using blood haemoglobin and haematocrit measurements (calculated % change [ 44 ], EKF Diagnostics Holdings plc, Cardiff, Wales, UK), urine specific gravity via refractometry (ratio, PAL-10S; ATAGO Co., Ltd; Tokyo, Japan), urine colour via eight-point visual scale (AU, [ 45 ]), plasma and urine osmolality via freezing point analysis (mmol.kg, Osmometer K-7400S, Knauer), fluid retention via calculation (%, urine mass subtracted from fluid mass ingested [300 g]). All measures are to be assessed at baseline and then 60-, 120- and 180-min post-ingestion.

Perceived responses to supplementation, as assessed through the following questionnaires. Changes in hunger, appetite, and thirst will be assessed at baseline and then 15-, 30-, 45-, 60-, 90-, 120- and 180-min post-ingestion using 0–100-point scales. Gastrointestinal symptoms will be assessed at the same time points, using Likert-type scales [ 46 ]. Immediately post-ingestion of test beverage, participants will also complete questionnaires regarding which supplement they believe they ingested, and the extent to which they enjoyed or tolerated ingesting that supplement. All questionnaires are provided as Appendices 2–5. Blood glucose (HemoCue® Glucose 201 +, Ängelholm, Sweden) and serum insulin (clinical assay, Human Insulin ELISA Kit, CrystalChem, Illinois, United States of America) will be analysed at baseline, and then 60-, 120- and 180-min post-ingestion.

During each of the four sessions, participants will consume two drink bottles containing 150 mL of fluid each, for a total volume of 300 mL per session. Participants will be instructed to consume the first bottle within five minutes, rest for five minutes, and then consume the second bottle within an additional five minutes. Drinks are to be stored and provided to participants at 4 degrees Celsius.

The four treatments are as follows: Almond protein powder (28 g protein content, 59 g of powder), topped up to 300 mL with almond milk Whey protein isolate powder (28 g protein content, 29 g of powder), topped up to 300 mL with almond milk Almond milk (300 mL) Water only (300 mL)

Almond protein powder (28 g protein content, 59 g of powder), topped up to 300 mL with almond milk

Whey protein isolate powder (28 g protein content, 29 g of powder), topped up to 300 mL with almond milk

Almond milk (300 mL)

Water only (300 mL)

All treatments, except water, will be chocolate-flavoured to minimise the influence of taste or familiarity on participants’ perceptual responses. The almond and whey protein powders will be mixed with almond milk to achieve a uniform final protein content of 28 g (protein content from the powder and milk combined). The almond milk treatment will also consist of a 60 g dose of maltodextrin, to replicate a placebo treatment from another study within this project. Treatments 3 and 4 are twin comparators, each serving the primary outcomes of this study. Almond milk operates as a comparator for APP and whey with respect to aminoacidemia measurements, and water operates as a comparator for APP with respect to hydration measurements. Macronutrient, energy, sodium and fibre composition of each substance and each treatment drink are reported in Table 1 , with additional ingredient details included in Appendix 6. As a crossover study, only the order in which the treatments are completed is to be randomised. Given the target sample size of 14, complete counterbalancing of orders is not feasible. Accordingly, we will employ randomisation based on a Williams Design [ 47 ] with slight modifications (sequence reversals) to increase the number of unique sequences to seven. Each sequence is randomly allocated to two participants each, using a computer-generated randomisation list (randomizer.org). See Fig. 3 below for example of this sequence randomisation outcome. Participants are partially blinded, given the water only treatment is not replicable for taste or texture as compared to the other three treatments. The other three treatments are matched for almond milk and chocolate powder flavouring, though texture of the protein powders and maltodextrin are not identical. Participants will complete a supplement belief questionnaire (Additional File 5), to assess if they were able to correctly and confidently identify the treatments of each session. Fig. 3 Williams Design randomisation of order of administration of treatments in the current study. Example treatments are A = almond protein powder, B = whey protein powder, C = almond milk, D = water

Williams Design randomisation of order of administration of treatments in the current study. Example treatments are A = almond protein powder, B = whey protein powder, C = almond milk, D = water

Data will be entered into Excel sheets during data collection sessions or obtained from Excel outputs from REDCap in the case of questionnaire data. All data are to be entered into two independent and identical data sheets by two members of the research team, with any errors corrected at the conclusion of data collection by verification with hard-copy data sheets completed during testing sessions. All data will be re-identifiable at the time of data collection. Reidentification will occur using unique coded identifiers, which will be assigned at the time of data collection. These coded identifiers will be stored on a password protected computer file on a Research Data Store (RDS) via network drive and in hard copy formats kept in a separate locked filing cabinet at Deakin University. This information, data and identifiers will only be accessible by members of the research team.

A primary analysis of intention to treat will be conducted of all the participants that have completed the trial. Between-treatment comparisons will be made using linear mixed models (LMMs) with a fixed effect of treatment and a random intercept for participant, adjusting for baseline outcome level within each period. Outcome variables will be transformed where necessary to satisfy parametric assumptions. Given subjective data from questionnaires often returns data distributions that are not normal, non-parametric equivalents of LMMs will be implemented where necessary (Mann–Whitney U-tests). Factors that will be accounted for in analyses include baseline hydration status (USG, total body water). All tests will be two-tailed with statistical significance set at p < 0.017 (i.e. nominal p < 0.017 with Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons of almond protein powder vs each of the three other treatments). The data will be analyzed by a blinded member of the research team who was not involved in the data collection.

DUHREC: 2024/ HE000669 , ANZCTR: ACTRN12625000127404p.
sections.discussion:
A primary strength of this study is the recruitment of postmenopausal women, an underrepresented population in exercise and nutrition research [ 48 ], and in clinical trials [ 49 ]. Design of protein supplementation strategy recommendations that are specific to this population may be expected to increase the likelihood of beneficial outcomes and adherence by consumers of protein supplements. The inclusion of hydration assessment addresses a particularly relevant factor for this demographic, who are more susceptible to under-hydration and hormone-related changes in fluid balance and thermoregulation [ 33 , 34 ]. This may offer a secondary benefit alongside the more conventionally observed benefits of protein supplementation, such as improved or maintained muscle function.

This study draws on both objective and subjective assessments, which reflects the decision-making process consumers may undertake when considering use of a supplement such as APP or whey. Specifically, assessing aminoacidemia and hydration alongside participant perceptions towards the interventions enables consideration of the physiological potential for desirable adaptations with the likelihood of adherence, based on factors such as taste, gastrointestinal symptoms, and supplement tolerability [ 50 ]. This study’s use of a randomised crossover design is a strength which allows each participant to serve as their own control. This approach minimises the effect of inter-individual variability, enhances statistical power, and enables precise comparisons between treatments. This is a particularly relevant strategy when working with an underrepresented population, such as postmenopausal women, where fewer data is available to compare and interpret across studies.

This study may face several challenges, inherent to the study design. As noted in Table 1 , there are some macronutrient and other discrepancies between the treatments, given that we have standardised for the protein content of the APP and whey protein treatments as an inherent and unavoidable part of this study focus and design. To facilitate hydration status comparisons, the water treatment is not a true placebo, in that it is not standardised to the other treatments for taste or appearance. MPS is not directly measured, rather circulating amino acid concentrations are utilised to represent potential anabolic effect. The acute nature of the study (up to three hours post-prandial only) limits the transferability to longer-term supplementation. Comparisons of APP to other commercially available plant-based protein supplements, such as pea protein or soy protein, may offer further value in future studies.

This study has received ethical approval from the Deakin University Human Research Ethics Committee (DUHREC 2024/ HE000669 ) and adheres to the National Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research (2023). Prior to commencement, all participants will be provided with a Plain Language Statement and additionally verbally briefed on the study requirements and will be asked to provide written informed consent if they wish to participate. Furthermore, verbal assent will also be reconfirmed during each individual trial. Participants will be free to withdraw from the study at any point, and this will not affect participant relationships with the associated researchers or Deakin University. All collected information will be labelled with a unique study code (de-identified), and not with name or any other identifying information, which will be kept separate from the information collected. It is the intention of the researchers to publish the results of this project. In such circumstances, participant identity will not be disclosed. In all cases, information will be provided in such a way that participants cannot be identified.

Recruitment of participants for this study commenced in May of 2025, and is continuing at the time of submission. Three of the required nine participants have been recruited. Data collection is therefore expected to complete in October 2025.
